To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the odds of a white-tailed deer migrating increased with the severity of winter conditions, whereas the odds of a deer being a resident increased with the density and size of forest patches in the landscape.
deer migration behavior varies with landscape characteristics and deer winter severity.

white-tailed deer exhibited 1 of 3 migration strategies (resident, conditional, and obligate), and landscape variables were associated with these migration strategies, with deer inhabiting areas with higher forest density and area as residents, deer inhabiting areas of higher winter severity as obligate migrants, and deer inhabiting areas in between these 2 extremes as conditional migrants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of landscape characteristics and deer density on the migration strategy of white-tailed (Odocoiles virginianus) deer.
the influence of landscape characteristics on the migration strategies of white‐tailed deer.
the influence of landscape characteristics on the migratory behavior of white-tail deer in the Upper Midwestern United States.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
deer migration is a complex phenomenon that varies with landscape characteristics, deer density, and deer winter severity.
deer in our study areas were influenced by a combination of landscape characteristics and deer winter severity to migrate, to be a resident, or to be a conditional migrant.
the probability of deer migration was negatively associated with forest density and positively associated with deer winter severity index and deer density.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
deer migration is a complex process and that the landscape characteristics we identified as important are only a subset of factors that influence migration behavior.

the odds of deer remaining residents or being obligate migrants increased as the density of forest patches and mean patch size increased, and the odds of migrating increased with increasing severity of winter conditions.
deer that live in areas with a lot of forest cover tend not to migrate, and those in more open areas tend to migrate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
deer in the Midwest and Great Plains are not a single population but rather several populations that differ in their migration strategies.
deer migration strategies vary among regions, and the landscape characteristics of deer wintering areas can be used to predict deer migration strategies.
deer that are residents in one region are not likely to migrate in another region, and vice versa.
